html:
Lapis lazuli is a deep blue stone flecked with gold coloured pyrite. For thousands of years nearly all of it came from mines in the Kokcha valley of Badakhshan, in the mountains of northeastern Afghanistan, and the mines still work today.

It is one of the oldest long distance trades we know. By around 3000 BCE lapis was reaching Mesopotamia and Egypt, thousands of kilometres away, passed from hand to hand across Iran.

  • The royal tombs of Ur held jewellery and statues inlaid with it.
  • Egyptian craftsmen used it for amulets and scarabs, and in the gold mask of Tutankhamun.
  • The Indus civilisation had a trading post at Shortugai, near the mines.

Ground into powder, lapis makes the pigment ultramarine. It coloured Buddhist wall paintings in Afghanistan, and later, carried west by Venetian traders, the robes of the Virgin Mary in European paintings, where it cost more than gold.
